content: Pimecrolimus was developed as an alternative treatment to topical corticosteroids for managing eczema, also known as atopic dermatitis. However, its effectiveness and safety compared to existing treatments remain uncertain. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of topical pimecrolimus in treating eczema. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to October 2006. They also reached out to researchers and manufacturers in the field. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared 1.0% topical pimecrolimus, applied twice daily, with other topical treatments for eczema. Two independent authors reviewed the studies for eligibility and extracted data related to efficacy, tolerability, and safety. A random-effects model was used to calculate pooled risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The analysis included 31 trials with a total of 8,019 participants. In short-term trials lasting six weeks or less, pimecrolimus cream was found to be significantly more effective and better tolerated than the vehicle cream (a cream base without pimecrolimus). In long-term trials lasting six months or more, pimecrolimus was significantly better than the vehicle cream in preventing eczema flares and improving quality of life. Specifically, in nine trials involving 3,091 participants, the risk ratio for preventing flares at six months was 1.47 (95% CI 1.32 to 1.64). However, pimecrolimus was less effective than two topical corticosteroids. For example, it was less effective than 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide based on investigators' global assessment in one trial with 658 participants (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.83). It was also less effective than 0.1% betamethasone valerate based on participants' global assessment in another trial with 87 participants (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.81) after three weeks of treatment. Additionally, pimecrolimus was associated with a higher rate of overall withdrawals and reports of skin burning. Importantly, none of the trials reported on key adverse effects such as skin thinning. When compared to 0.1% tacrolimus, pimecrolimus was significantly less effective based on investigators' global assessment at six weeks (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.74). It also led to more withdrawals due to lack of efficacy (RR 2.37, 95% CI 1.10 to 5.08) in two trials involving 639 participants. However, there was no significant difference in the proportion of participants experiencing any adverse events between the two treatments. In conclusion, topical pimecrolimus is less effective than moderate and potent corticosteroids, as well as 0.1% tacrolimus. Its therapeutic role remains uncertain due to the lack of key comparisons with mild corticosteroids.
